title: Wattles and grevilleas

names.gloss: a spear point made from wattle and used for turtle spearing. it was put in the fire until it was hard enough to pierce through a turtle shell.

scientificName: Acacia guymeri, A. holosericea, A. leptostachya and the other wattles; Grevillea parallela, G. glauca, G. pteridifolia

identification.basis: The dictionary names a white wattle, a black wattle with a yellow flower, a wattle species and the fire-hardened wattle spear point. Within 30 km of Karma Waters the Atlas has 21 wattles, headed by Acacia guymeri, the candelabra wattle and the Townsville wattle, and three grevilleas.

summary: **[yalngkal](word:yalngkal)** is the 'white wattle', **[yarun](word:yarun)** the 'black wattle (yellow flower)' and **[yumba](word:yumba)** a 'species of wattle'; **[kurrajan](word:kurrajan)** is 'a spear point made from wattle and used for turtle spearing. It was put in the fire until it was hard enough to pierce through a turtle shell', and the water of cooked wattle bark is the dictionary's cure for the [poison nut's](entry:leaching) burn [ref:hershberger1982]. The wattles are the understorey of the Karma Waters [woodland](entry:woodland): twenty-one kinds within 30 km, headed by *Acacia guymeri* with twenty-six records, 'an open, single stemmed or multistemmed shrub with smooth, silver-grey bark' that is 'near threatened' in Queensland, the silky **candelabra wattle** with its 'tightly and sometimes irregularly coiled pods', and the **Townsville wattle** with 'spikes of golden yellow flowers' in August and September [ref:ala-karma-plants] [ref:wiki-guymeri] [ref:wiki-holosericea] [ref:wiki-leptostachya]. Wattle was the hard wood of the kit: Anderson's table of Kuku Yalanji spears has 'wood (*Acacia* sp)' for the heads of the fighting and fishing spears, the harpoon point was 'a sharpened and fire-hardened point some 10 cm–15 cm long made from *Acacia crassicarpa*', and the candelabra wattle was a [fish poison](entry:fish-poisoning) [ref:anderson1996] [ref:wiki-holosericea]. Wattle seed is the other thing: 'wattleseeds were a relatively recent addition to Aboriginal Australian diets with specialized seed grinders first dated to 1000 years ago. Many species require pre-treatment of seeds through parching at high temperatures, soaking, or cracking' [ref:wiki-wattleseed]. The **grevilleas** beside them, the silver oak, bushman's clothes peg and the golden grevillea, gave the gum that cemented spear heads and axe hafts and the charcoal for paint, and give the honeyeaters and the [bees](entry:native-bees) their flowers from the dry season on [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1909] [ref:wiki-pteridifolia].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[yalngkal](word:yalngkal)** 'white wattle'; **[yarun](word:yarun)** 'black wattle (yellow flower)' and 'black wattle tree and its yellow flower'; **[yumba](word:yumba)** 'species of wattle; wattle tree'. **[kurrajan](word:kurrajan)** 'a spear point made from wattle and used for turtle spearing. It was put in the fire until it was hard enough to pierce through a turtle shell' (the Nyungkul point is *biyul*). **[jinjay](word:jinjay)** 'poison nut tree ... the bark and sap are poisonous, but water from cooked wattle tree bark will cure the poisoned skin' [ref:hershberger1982]. 'Wattle' is the colonists' word, from the wattle-and-daub huts they built of acacia saplings; which of the twenty-one Karma Waters wattles is *yalngkal* and which *yarun* is not recorded. The golden grevillea carries its own Aboriginal names from the west and north, '*manbulu*, *yawuny* and *tjummula*' [ref:wiki-pteridifolia].

sections.heading: The wattles and grevilleas of the upper Mitchell
sections.body:
***Acacia guymeri***, twenty-six records, the commonest. 'An open, single or multistemmed shrub that typically grows to a height of 1–2.5 m and has smooth, silver-grey bark. Its branchlets are red-brown or yellowish red, resinous and covered with minute scales. The phyllodes are linear ... 80–160 mm long, 1–2 mm wide'; 'the flowers are pale yellow or golden yellow and borne in spikes 9–13 mm long. Flowering has been recorded in January'; 'this species of wattle grows in poor soil on rocky ridges and in disturbed areas and in *Eucalyptus* woodland from west of Cooktown in the north extending down the western edge of the Great Dividing Range to near Mount Surprise'; 'listed as "near threatened" under the Queensland Government *Nature Conservation Act 1992*' [ref:wiki-guymeri].

**Candelabra wattle, soapbush, silver wattle** (*A. holosericea*), seven records. 'A shrub or tree that typically grows to 3–8 m high ... and has branchlets and young shoots covered with silvery, silky hairs'; phyllodes 'obliquely narrowly elliptic, 100–200 mm long, 20–50 mm wide and usually covered with silky hairs'; 'the flowers are golden yellow and borne in rod-like spikes'; 'the pods are tightly and somewhat irregularly coiled ... remaining as entangled clumps after the seeds have been released. The seeds are oblong, 3.5 mm long, shiny dark brown with a bright yellow aril'; 'found in and around ephemeral watercourses growing in gravelly sand or loamy soils' [ref:wiki-holosericea]. The [fish-poison plants](entry:fish-poison-plants) page has its use, and 'soapbush' is the other: the crushed phyllodes lather.

**Townsville wattle, slender wattle** (*A. leptostachya*), six records. 'A shrub or tree that typically grows to a height of 0.5–6 m'; 'the flowers are golden yellow and borne in two spikes 20–40 mm long'; 'flowering occurs in August and September'; 'grows in deep sand on sandstone or granite in eucalypt woodland, open forest or *Triodia* hummock grassland' [ref:wiki-leptostachya]. Beside these the Atlas list has *A. ammitia*, *A. chisholmii*, *A. humifusa*, *A. julifera*, *A. simsii*, *A. flavescens*, *A. disparrima*, *A. multisiliqua*, *A. victoriae* and more, and two *Vachellia* [ref:ala-karma-plants].

**The grevilleas.** The [woodland](entry:woodland) page describes the **silver oak** (*Grevillea parallela*), thirteen records, 'to 15 m with dark furrowed bark and hanging strap leaves', and **bushman's clothes peg** (*G. glauca*), nine, 'spindly, hairy-leaved, with cylinders of flowers' [ref:wiki-parallela] [ref:wiki-glauca]. The **golden grevillea** (*G. pteridifolia*), two records: 'a shrub or tree that typically grows to a height of 2–14 m'; leaves 'usually pinnatisect with 13 to 29 linear ... lobes'; 'the flowers are greyish-green to silvery on the outside, the inside and the style bright orange-yellow or reddish'; 'flowering occurs in most months with a peak from May to September'; 'plants from Queensland are non-lignotuberous shrubs to small trees with smooth bark'; it was 'first collected by Europeans from the vicinity of the Endeavour River' by Banks and Solander in 1770 [ref:wiki-pteridifolia]. Grevilleas generally are 'commonly known as spider flowers', 'the fruit a follicle that splits down one side only, releasing one or two seeds' [ref:wiki-grevillea].

**What they were for.** Anderson's table of Kuku Yalanji spears gives 'wood (*Acacia* sp)' as the material of the heads of the *yirrmba* fishing spear, the *dikarra* and *kuyan* fighting spears and the *dajal*; the turtle harpoon's point was 'a sharpened and fire-hardened point some 10 cm–15 cm long made from *Acacia crassicarpa* or sometimes *Erythrophloeum*'; and '*Acacia holocarpa*' made the distal tips of other spears; see [spear and woomera](entry:spear-and-woomera) [ref:anderson1996]. Meat went into the [earth oven](entry:earth-oven) 'with *Eucalyptus*, *Acacia* or wild ginger leaves for' flavour [ref:anderson1996]. For the grevilleas, Anderson lists '*Grevillea striata*' gum among the resins 'widely used' for 'fixing spear points and axe hafts', and 'Grevillea charcoal' with the ochres and kaolin as 'the major sources of paint' [ref:anderson1996]; Roth's spear-throwers were lashed 'with tendon under *Grevillea* cement' [ref:roth1909]. Wattle seed: 'wattleseeds were a relatively recent addition to Aboriginal Australian diets with specialized seed grinders first dated to 1000 years ago. Many species require pre-treatment of seeds through parching at high temperatures, soaking, or cracking using seed grinders. Following the colonization of Australia, consumption of wattleseed decreased but was not eliminated', and 'acacia seed flour has recently gained popularity in Australia due to its high nutritional content, hardiness, and low toxicity' [ref:wiki-wattleseed].

sections.heading: Telling the wattles and grevilleas
sections.body:
- ***A. guymeri***: needle-thin phyllodes, silver-grey smooth bark, resinous red twigs, on the stony ridges [ref:wiki-guymeri].
- **Candelabra wattle**: broad silky-silver phyllodes, rod flowers, coiled tangled pods, by the creeks [ref:wiki-holosericea].
- **Townsville wattle**: narrow phyllodes with many fine veins, paired golden spikes in August, on deep sand [ref:wiki-leptostachya].
- **Silver oak**: a tree with hanging strap leaves and furrowed bark [ref:wiki-parallela].
- **Bushman's clothes peg**: broad hairy leaves and a woody fruit split like a peg [ref:wiki-glauca].
- **Golden grevillea**: fern-like divided leaves, silky beneath, and orange toothbrush flowers [ref:wiki-pteridifolia].
- **Not a wattle**: the [kurrajong](entry:kurrajong) and [cotton tree](entry:cotton-tree) have lobed leaves; the [ironwood](entry:ironwood) is a legume too but a big dark tree with poisonous leaves.

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Yellow blossom on the ridges** in the dry: the wattles, and the honeyeaters and bees in them [ref:wiki-leptostachya].
- **Orange toothbrush flowers** from May: the golden grevillea, with the lorikeets and honeyeaters on it [ref:wiki-pteridifolia] [ref:wiki-bfh].
- **Coiled pods in tangles** on the ground under a silver shrub: the candelabra wattle's seed [ref:wiki-holosericea].
- **Gum beads** on a grevillea's trunk: the cement [ref:anderson1996].
- **Wattles dead after a hot fire** on the stony ironbark ridges: that woodland is burnt only every 10–50 years because 'its wattles do not survive frequent or hot fire' [ref:re-9-11-1].

sections.heading: Where they grow
sections.body: *A. guymeri* 'in poor soil on rocky ridges'; the candelabra wattle 'in and around ephemeral watercourses'; the Townsville wattle 'in deep sand on sandstone or granite'; the grevilleas through the open [woodland](entry:woodland), the silver oak and clothes peg among its commonest small trees [ref:wiki-guymeri] [ref:wiki-holosericea] [ref:wiki-leptostachya] [ref:ala-karma-plants].

sections.heading: The understorey
sections.body: The wattles and grevilleas are the woodland's second storey and its blossom between the gums' flowerings: the wattles' pollen for the [native bees](entry:native-bees), the grevilleas' nectar for the honeyeaters, lorikeets and [flying foxes](entry:flying-foxes-and-bats), the wattle seed for the [parrots](entry:cockatoos-and-parrots), 'seeds of eucalyptus, acacia', and the ants that carry the seeds' yellow arils away and plant them [ref:wiki-holosericea] [ref:wiki-bfh]. The wattles fix nitrogen in the poor stony soil, which is part of why the woodland grows at all, and their death in a hot fire is the Herbarium's reason for burning the stony ridges rarely [ref:re-9-11-1].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: The Townsville wattle flowers in August and September, *A. guymeri* in January, the golden grevillea 'with a peak from May to September'; the wattle seed ripens in the late dry and the build-up; the spear-wood is cut any time [ref:wiki-leptostachya] [ref:wiki-guymeri] [ref:wiki-pteridifolia]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Spear heads, barbs and harpoon points**, fire-hardened: *kurrajan* [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996].
- **Fish poison**: the candelabra wattle; see [fish poisoning](entry:fish-poisoning) [ref:wiki-holosericea].
- **Seed flour** from the wattles that bear it, parched, cracked and ground; see [wild rice and grass seed](entry:wild-rice-and-grass-seed) [ref:wiki-wattleseed].
- **Bark water** for skin poisoned by the poison nut's sap; see [bush medicine](entry:bush-medicine) [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Leaves** in the earth oven with the meat [ref:anderson1996].
- **Gum**: wattle gum to eat and to glue; grevillea gum as cement for spear heads and axe hafts; see [beeswax and gums](entry:beeswax-and-gums) [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1909].
- **Grevillea charcoal** for paint, with the ochres [ref:anderson1996].
- **Soap**: the candelabra wattle's phyllodes, the 'soapbush' [ref:wiki-holosericea].

sections.heading: A fire-hardened wattle point, and wattle seed
sections.body:
1. **Choose a straight wattle branch** of dense wood about a thumb thick, and cut and shave a point 10–15 cm long, as Anderson's harpoon points were [ref:anderson1996].
2. **Harden it in the fire**: hold the point in the hot ashes, turning it, until it is charred brown and hard, not burnt; 'it was put in the fire until it was hard enough to pierce through a turtle shell' [ref:hershberger1982].
3. **Fix it** with gum and twine; see [spear and woomera](entry:spear-and-woomera) and [beeswax and gums](entry:beeswax-and-gums) [ref:roth1909].
4. **Seed**: gather the pods when they split, parch the seed on a hot flat stone or in a bark dish of coals, winnow, crack and grind on the [stone](entry:stone); 'many species require pre-treatment of seeds through parching at high temperatures, soaking, or cracking' [ref:wiki-wattleseed].
5. **Know your wattle**: not every acacia's seed is food, the candelabra wattle is a fish poison, and the bark-water remedy is the dictionary's, not a tested one [ref:wiki-holosericea] [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- The candelabra wattle is a fish poison; keep it out of the drinking water [ref:wiki-holosericea].
- *A. guymeri* is near threatened; take spear wood from the common wattles [ref:wiki-guymeri].
- Native plants are protected; gathering for personal use on native title country is covered by the Western Yalanji determinations [ref:qld-nca] [ref:alrc] [ref:wyac2020].
- A fire-hardened point is a weapon; see [spear and woomera](entry:spear-and-woomera).

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The wattles and grevilleas are under every ironbark on Karma Waters, and the golden grevillea's orange flowers are the dry season's colour on the ridges [ref:ala-karma-plants] [ref:wiki-pteridifolia]. Which is *yalngkal* and which *yarun* here is for the contribution box below [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: *[yalngkal](word:yalngkal)* 'white wattle'; *[yarun](word:yarun)* 'black wattle (yellow flower)'; *[yumba](word:yumba)* 'wattle tree'; *[kurrajan](word:kurrajan)* fire-hardened wattle spear point; *[jinjay](word:jinjay)* 'poison nut tree'; *[juku](word:juku)* 'tree, wood'; *[baya](word:baya)* 'fire, firewood'; *[jila](word:jila)* 'beeswax' [ref:hershberger1982].
